For three days you have asked questions of tables that behaved themselves. Today you meet one
that does not.

Real environmental data arrives with holes in it, with the same sample entered twice, and with
numbers stored as text. None of that is a mistake anyone made. It is what happens when
sixteen thousand measurements are pooled from thirty-seven separate studies over thirty-five
years. Your job is not to be annoyed by it. Your job is to find it, decide what to do about
it, and write down what you decided.

Today's dataset is NOAA's marine microplastics archive, and you will be with it all day: this
morning to clean it, this afternoon to transform it, and the end-of-day practice to answer
questions with it.

By the end of this session you will be able to:

- count what is missing, and say which columns are missing it
- remove rows with `.dropna()`, and say why the bare version is almost always wrong
- fill gaps with `.fillna(value)` when removal would cost too much
- find duplicated rows with `.duplicated()`, and drop them with `.drop_duplicates()`
- read a column's dtype and change it with `.astype()`

## What is missing

You met this sentence on Day 2. It is the first thing to run on a table you did not create:

```{python}
plastics.isnull().sum()
```

Five columns have holes in them. Two of the holes are enormous:

```{python}
plastics.isnull().sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5)
```

`SubRegions` is missing on 15,657 rows out of 16,245, and `Regions` on 8,249. `Measurement`,
which is the actual number this whole archive exists to record, is missing on 5,792.

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 `.isnull()` returns a `True`/`False` for every cell, and `.sum()` counts the `True`s, one
column at a time. It is the same "add up a mask" trick you used on Day 3 when you counted rows
that passed a filter.
:::

## Dropping rows: `.dropna()`

The obvious move is to throw away the incomplete rows. `.dropna()` does that:

```{python}
plastics.dropna().shape
```

**588 rows.** You started with 16,245 and kept 3.6% of them.

That is not a cleaning step. That is destroying the dataset. And notice how quietly it
happened: one method, no arguments, no warning, no error message.

:::{.callout-important title="Bare `.dropna()` is almost always the wrong tool"}
With no arguments, `.dropna()` removes every row that has a missing value **in any column at
all**. Here, a sample with a perfectly good measurement gets deleted because nobody recorded
its `SubRegions`.

The fix is to say which columns you actually care about.
:::

## Dropping on purpose: `.dropna(subset=[...])`

`subset=` takes a **list** of column names, and only those columns can get a row deleted:

```{python}
measured = plastics.dropna(subset=['Measurement'])
measured.shape
```

10,453 rows. That is a defensible cleaning step and a terrible one, and which it is depends
entirely on a question you have not asked yet.

Ask it now. Compare the units before and after:

```{python}
plastics['Unit'].value_counts()
```

```{python}
measured['Unit'].value_counts()
```

An entire unit vanished. All 5,792 `pieces/10 mins` samples had a missing `Measurement`, so
dropping on `Measurement` deleted every one of them, and with them every sample taken by the
one study that used that method.

:::{.callout-important title="Missing values are rarely scattered at random"}
On Day 2 you learned that `value` columns stack incompatible units. This is the other half of
that lesson: **missingness is itself a variable**. Here it lines up exactly with sampling
method, so a filter that looks like it removes bad rows actually removes one team's entire
field campaign.

Before you drop anything, count what you are dropping and look at what it has in common.
:::

That does not mean you should keep them. If you are about to average measurements, rows with no
measurement are useless to you. It means you should be able to say, out loud, *what* you
removed, and record it in your notebook.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
`Oceans` is missing on 271 rows. Use `.dropna()` with `subset=` to build a table called
`located` that has none of them, and report its shape. Then check whether those 271 rows had
anything in common: compare `plastics['Unit'].value_counts()` with the same call on `located`.
:::

## Filling gaps: `.fillna(value)`

Sometimes the missing value means something, and removing the row throws that meaning away.
`Regions` is missing on 8,249 rows not because anyone forgot, but because the sample was in
open ocean, outside any named sea.

`.fillna()` replaces the gaps with a value you choose:

```{python}
plastics['Regions'] = plastics['Regions'].fillna('Unspecified')
plastics['Regions'].value_counts().head(5)
```

Two things worth noticing in that one line. `.fillna()` hangs off a **column**, not the whole
table. And it returns a new column, so you have to assign it back to `plastics['Regions']` for
the change to stick. That is the same rule you have met every day this week: pandas hands you a
result, and it is yours to keep or to discard.

```{python}
plastics.isnull().sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3)
```

`Regions` is now at zero.

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 Choose your fill value on purpose. `'Unspecified'` is honest: it says "we know this is
blank." Filling with `0` would have been a lie, because zero is a real measurement. Never fill
a numeric column with a number that could be mistaken for data.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
`SubRegions` is missing on 15,657 rows. Fill it with `'Unspecified'`, assign the result back,
and re-run `plastics.isnull().sum()` to confirm it worked. Then, in a markdown cell, say
whether filling or dropping was the right call for that column, and why.
:::

## Duplicated rows

The other classic defect is the same sample entered twice. `.duplicated()` returns a mask, one
`True` or `False` per row, and `.sum()` counts them:

```{python}
plastics.duplicated().sum()
```

Zero. Clean data, then.

Except no. Look at the columns again:

```{python}
plastics[['OBJECTID', 'GlobalID', 'Latitude', 'Longitude', 'Date', 'Measurement']].head(3)
```

`OBJECTID` and `GlobalID` are identifiers, assigned one per record when the archive was built.
No two rows can ever share them, so no two rows can ever be identical, so `.duplicated()` can
only ever return zero. The answer was never about the data.

`subset=` fixes this the same way it fixed `.dropna()`. Point it at the columns that hold the
science:

```{python}
sample_columns = ['Latitude', 'Longitude', 'Date', 'Measurement', 'Unit']
plastics.duplicated(subset=sample_columns).sum()
```

856 rows record the same measurement, in the same unit, at the same coordinates, on the same
day, as some earlier row.

:::{.callout-important title="`.duplicated()` is only as good as the columns you point it at"}
This is the single most common way people convince themselves a dataset is clean. Any table
with an auto-generated ID column will report zero duplicates forever.

Decide what "the same observation" means for *your* data, put those column names in a list, and
pass the list to `subset=`.
:::

`.drop_duplicates()` takes the same argument and returns a table with the repeats removed,
keeping the first of each:

```{python}
deduplicated = plastics.drop_duplicates(subset=sample_columns)
deduplicated.shape
```

Now the hard part, which pandas cannot do for you. Are those 856 rows really duplicates? Two
tows through the same patch of water on the same day, both finding zero pieces per cubic metre,
would look exactly like this and would both be real:

```{python}
repeats = plastics[plastics.duplicated(subset=sample_columns, keep=False)]
repeats[['Measurement', 'Unit', 'Sampling Method', 'Short Reference']].head(6)
```

```{python}
(repeats['Measurement'] == 0).sum()
```

Of the 1,465 rows involved, 652 report a measurement of zero. That is a strong hint that many
of these are genuine repeat samples which happened to agree, rather than double entries, so we
will **keep** them and say so in the notebook.

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 `keep=False` marks *every* member of a duplicated group, not just the later ones. Use it
when you want to look at duplicates; use the default when you want to drop them.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Build a different list of columns that you think defines "the same observation" here, and count
the duplicates it finds. Try dropping `Measurement` from the list, or adding
`Sampling Method`. Write one sentence in a markdown cell saying which definition you would
defend to a reviewer.
:::

## Types: reading them and changing them

Every column has a **dtype**, which is what pandas believes the column contains:

```{python}
plastics.dtypes
```

`float64` is a decimal number, `int64` a whole number, and `object` is pandas saying "text, or
something I could not identify." Three of these are wrong for what the column means.

`Accession Number` is stored as an integer:

```{python}
plastics['Accession Number'].head(3)
```

It is not a quantity. Nobody will ever add two accession numbers together or take their mean.
It is a label that happens to be spelled with digits, and leaving it numeric invites pandas to
average it for you in some later summary. `.astype()` converts a column to the type you name:

```{python}
plastics['Accession Number'] = plastics['Accession Number'].astype(str)
plastics['Accession Number'].head(3)
```

```{python}
plastics['Accession Number'].dtype
```

`object`, which is what text looks like. The same assign-it-back rule applies: `.astype()`
returns a converted column and changes nothing until you store it.

The three conversions you will use all week are `.astype(float)`, `.astype(int)`, and
`.astype(str)`:

```{python}
plastics['Latitude'].astype(int).head(3)
```

That one is a demonstration, not a suggestion. `.astype(int)` truncates toward zero, so
-58.4283 becomes -58, and nearly half a degree of latitude, about 47 kilometres, is gone.
Converting to a narrower type throws information away, silently.

:::{.callout-caution title="`.astype()` fails loudly on text it cannot parse"}
If a numeric column has even one entry like `'not recorded'`, `.astype(float)` raises a
`ValueError` naming the offending value. That is pandas doing you a favour. Read the value it
names, fix that, and convert again.

You will meet exactly this in the colab this afternoon.
:::

`Date` is an `object` too, because it is text like `2/3/2017 12:00:00 AM`. Dates are their own
subject and they get a whole session on Day 6, so leave that one alone for now.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Convert `OBJECTID` to text with `.astype(str)`, assign it back, and confirm the change with
`.dtype`. Then, in a markdown cell, name one other column in this table whose dtype does not
match what the column means, and say what it should be.
:::

## Putting it together

A cleaning pass is a short, ordered list of decisions, each one a line of code with a comment
saying why:

```{python}
clean = plastics.copy()

# Open-ocean samples have no named region; that is information, not a gap.
clean['SubRegions'] = clean['SubRegions'].fillna('Unspecified')

# Accession numbers are labels, not quantities.
clean['Accession Number'] = clean['Accession Number'].astype(str)

# Keep only samples that carry a measurement. This drops all 5,792 'pieces/10 mins'
# rows, which is acceptable here because we are about to average measurements.
clean = clean.dropna(subset=['Measurement'])

clean.shape
```

```{python}
clean.isnull().sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3)
```

Four lines, three decisions, and a note in the code saying what the third one cost. If a
colleague asks you next month why your row count is 10,453 and not 16,245, the answer is right
there.

## Key points

- Run `df.isnull().sum()` first, every time, on any table you did not build yourself.
- Bare `.dropna()` deletes a row for a gap in **any** column. Here that cost 96% of the data.
  Use `.dropna(subset=['col'])` and name the columns you actually need.
- Before you drop, **count what you are dropping and look at what it has in common.**
  Missingness usually lines up with something.
- `.fillna(value)` replaces gaps with a value you choose. Choose one that cannot be mistaken
  for data.
- `.duplicated()` and `.drop_duplicates()` both take `subset=[...]`. Without it, any table with
  an ID column reports zero duplicates forever.
- `.astype(str/int/float)` converts a column. It returns a new column, so assign it back, and
  remember that narrowing a type throws information away.
